# Experiments That Outlive Their Experimenters

In a glass case at the University of Queensland, a funnel of tar has been dripping since 1930. Pitch looks solid. You can shatter it with a hammer. But it is actually a liquid, roughly a hundred billion times more viscous than water, and it takes about a decade for a single drop to form and fall.

The physicist Thomas Parnell set it up to show his students that appearances deceive. He died in 1948, having seen only two drops fall, neither of them while he was watching. The experiment passed to others, and eventually to John Mainstone, who looked after it for fifty-two years. Mainstone never saw a drop fall either. He missed one in 1977 by stepping away for a weekend. In 1988 he left the room for five minutes to get a drink. In 2000 a webcam was trained on it, and at the crucial moment the camera failed. Mainstone died in August 2013. The ninth drop fell the following April.

I keep coming back to this story, and I don't think it's because it's sad, although it is a little. It's because the experiment is, in a sense, working exactly as intended. Its lesson was never really about tar. It's about the scale of time on which the world actually operates, and how poorly that scale matches the span of a human life, or a human attention span.

---

There are others like it. At Michigan State University, a botanist named William James Beal buried twenty bottles of seeds in 1879, filled with sand and mixed with seeds of about twenty-one plant species. He wanted to know how long seeds could lie dormant in soil and still germinate. Every so often, someone digs up a bottle, plants the contents, and waits. The schedule has stretched over the years, from every five years to every ten to every twenty. The most recent bottle was dug up in 2021, at night so the seeds wouldn't see sunlight too soon. A few still sprouted, 142 years after Beal sealed them in. The next dig is planned for 2040. The last bottle, if the schedule holds, won't come up until 2100.

At Rothamsted in England, a field called Broadbalk has been sown with winter wheat almost every year since 1843, with different strips receiving different fertilizer treatments. It was started by John Bennet Lawes and Joseph Henry Gilbert, and it is now one of the oldest continuously running experiments in the world. Its data has been useful in ways its founders could not possibly have imagined. They didn't know about nitrogen isotopes, or atmospheric sulfur pollution, or soil microbiomes. The archived soil samples have been used to study all of these. The founders asked one question, and the field kept answering questions nobody had thought to ask yet.

---

What strikes me about these projects is the peculiar kind of trust they require. Beal was trusting people who weren't born yet to care about his bottles, to not lose the map, to not pave over the site, to remember the procedure. Lawes and Gilbert were trusting that the institution would survive, that funding would continue, that some future person would look at a wheat field and think *this is worth not changing*.

That last part may be the hardest. The natural impulse of any new custodian is to improve things, to modernize the method or fix the obvious flaws. And sometimes that's right. But a long-running experiment derives almost all of its value from continuity. The data from 1843 is precious precisely because the field in 2024 is being treated the same way. A change that seems sensible to one generation can quietly destroy the thing that made the project worth inheriting.

So these experiments are also experiments in a certain kind of humility. Every custodian is a link, not an endpoint. Mainstone spent half a century tending something he knew he might never see complete, and he did it anyway, and the drop fell, and the world found out about it partly because he'd kept it going.

---

I think there's something here that applies well beyond science. Most of what matters happens on time scales that are awkward for us. Forests, languages, institutions, trust between people, the slow accretion of knowledge: none of these can be seen changing in the moment. You can stare at pitch all day and it looks solid. You step out for a drink and miss everything.

The temptation, faced with slow things, is to conclude that nothing is happening, or that nothing we do matters because we won't see the result. The long experiments make the opposite case. Something is always happening. The question is whether anyone is keeping records, and whether they'll hand the records on.

There's a quieter consolation in them too. Parnell never saw a drop fall. Beal never saw most of his bottles opened. Lawes and Gilbert never saw what their soil would reveal. And yet it would be strange to say their work was incomplete or wasted. They set something in motion that was larger than they were, and they were at peace, apparently, with being its beginning rather than its conclusion.

Somewhere in Queensland, right now, the tenth drop is slowly forming. Probably no one is watching at this exact moment. It doesn't need anyone to. It's just going to keep falling, at its own pace, whether or not we're paying attention. The only real question is whether someone will be there to write it down.

Actually, I like the idea of writing about the longest-running scientific experiments—the pitch drop experiment, the Oxford Electric Bell ringing since 1840, the Beal seed experiment dug up every twenty years.
